question:
Complete the line so that it creates a Dog object and runs the Dog constructor:
Dog rex = ___ Dog("Rex");
correct: new
feedback: new creates the object and runs the constructor; rex then holds a reference to the finished object. Leave the word out and the line does not compile, because Dog("Rex") on its own looks like a call to a method named Dog. Declaring just  Dog rex;  creates no object at all: a local variable written that way has no value yet (the compiler will not let you read it), and a field written that way holds null.

correct: Once for each new Potion(...) expression, as that object is being created
incorrect: Once when the program starts, before main, to prepare the Potion class
Each time a method is called on a Potion, so that its fields are set first
Once, for the first Potion; later Potions reuse the values it set up
feedback: Potion(int doses) is a constructor: it has the class's name and no return type, and Java runs it as part of every new Potion(...). Three new expressions mean three separate runs, each filling in the fields of a different object. It is not a start-up routine for the class, it does not run again when you call methods on the object, and nothing is shared between one Potion and the next.

question: Which statements about constructors are true?
correct: A constructor has the same name as its class
A class may declare several constructors if their parameter lists differ
If a class declares no constructor, the compiler supplies one that takes no arguments
incorrect: A constructor is declared with the return type void, because it returns nothing
Java still supplies a no-argument constructor after you write one that takes parameters
A constructor can be called again on an existing object to reset it, as in rex.Dog("Max")
feedback: A constructor is named after its class and has NO return type at all. That matters: write  void Dog() { ... }  and it still compiles, but as an ordinary method that happens to be called Dog, so new Dog() never runs it and the fields keep their defaults. A class can have several constructors with different parameter lists. The free no-argument constructor exists only while you have written none: add Dog(String name) and  new Dog()  stops compiling. And a constructor runs only as part of new; rex.Dog("Max") is not legal, so resetting an object is a job for a method.

question: NPC: The assignment that does nothing
intro: Zoya the Golem-Shaper sets a small clay golem on the bench. It does not move. “Seven runes of power I gave it,” they say, “and it has none. Read my class with me.”

steps.say: Every golem I shape is one object, and the class Golem says each object has a field called power. Inside the constructor there are TWO things named power: the parameter and the field. When a name could mean either, the nearer one wins, so plain power means the parameter.

beats.say: Every golem I shape is one object. The class says each Golem object has a field called power.
Inside the constructor there are TWO things named power: the parameter and the field. The nearer one wins, so plain power means the parameter. We say the parameter shadows the field.

steps.say: So  power = power;  copies the parameter into itself. The field is never touched — and a field nobody assigns keeps its default value. For an int field that default is 0.

wrong: Nothing — the class does not compile
check.why: It compiles fine, which is what makes this bug nasty. The 7 was copied onto itself and thrown away; the field still holds its default, 0.

steps.say: The cure is the keyword this, which means the object being built right now. this.power is that object's field; plain power is still the parameter. Defaults to remember: number fields start at 0, boolean fields at false, and fields that refer to objects, such as a String, start at null.

beats.say: The cure is the keyword this. It means “the object being built right now”, so this.power is that object's field.
Keep the defaults in mind too: a number field starts at 0, a boolean field at false, and a field that refers to an object — a String, say — starts at null.

outro: “The next monster made my mistake with a String field. Decide what each field really holds before you answer.”

question: One of the two assignments in this constructor does nothing. What does the program print?
correct: null 5
feedback: Inside the constructor, name means the parameter, because the parameter shadows the field of the same name. name = name; copies the parameter onto itself, so the field keeps the default for a String field, null. The second assignment is fine: the parameter is called lvl, so level can only mean the field, which becomes 5. Writing this.name = name; fixes the bug.

question: A constructor has a parameter named hp, and its class has a field that is also named hp. Write the statement that stores the parameter in the field.
correct: this.hp = hp;
feedback: this.hp is the field of the object being built; plain hp is the parameter, because a parameter shadows a field with the same name. The field goes on the left since that is where the value is stored. hp = hp; compiles but changes nothing, and hp = this.hp; copies in the wrong direction, overwriting the parameter with the field's default.

question: Each line declares a field that no constructor ever assigns. Match each field to what is shown when it is printed.
feedback: Java fills every field of a new object with a default before the constructor runs: 0 for whole-number types, 0.0 for double, false for boolean, and null for any field that refers to an object — String included. A String field does not start as an empty string; it starts as null, meaning it refers to no object at all.

correct: It does not compile: the local variable gems was never given a value
incorrect: It prints 0 twice, because an int starts at 0 wherever it is declared
It does not compile: the field coins has no starting value
It compiles and prints 0, then throws an exception when gems is read
feedback: Default values are a privilege of fields. coins is a field, so it quietly starts at 0 and printing it is legal. gems is a local variable, and locals get no default: the compiler reports that gems might not have been initialized and refuses to build the class. Because the compiler catches it, nothing is left to go wrong while the program runs.

question:
Put in order, first to last, what happens when Java runs this line:
Dog rex = new Dog("Rex");
items: Memory is set aside for one new Dog object
The new object's fields are filled with default values
The constructor body runs and assigns the fields
A reference to the finished object is stored in rex
feedback: The right-hand side is finished before the assignment happens. new first makes room for the object and fills its fields with defaults, which is why a constructor that forgets a field leaves 0, false or null behind. Then the constructor body runs. Only when the object is complete does = store a reference to it in rex.

question: This class has two constructors, and one of them hands the work to the other. What does the program print?
feedback: Java picks the constructor whose parameter list matches the arguments. new Potion("Elixir") matches the one-parameter constructor, and this(name, 3) inside it runs the two-parameter constructor of the same class with doses = 3. q calls the two-parameter constructor directly with 5. Chaining with this(...) keeps the real set-up code in one place. (Older Java insisted that this(...) open the constructor; Java 25 allows other statements ahead of it, provided they do not use the object being built.)

question: Two Counter objects are created from the same class. What does the program print?
feedback: count is an instance field, so each object made with new carries its own copy. new ran twice, which makes two objects and two separate counts: a's is raised twice and b's once. Nothing done to one object reaches the other.

question: NPC: Two tags, one chest
intro: Zoya ties a paper tag marked a to the handle of an iron chest, then ties a second tag, marked b, to the same handle. “This,” they say, “is the one picture of objects I need you to keep.”

steps.say: new ran once, so there is one Chest object. A variable like a does not contain the chest. It holds a reference: a tag tied to the object, telling Java where to find it. b = a copies the tag, not the chest.

beats.say: Count how many times new runs here.

beats.code:
Chest a = new Chest();
Chest b = a;

beats.say: Once — so there is ONE Chest object. The variable a does not contain the chest. It holds a reference: a tag tied to the object, telling Java where to find it.
b = a copies the tag, not the chest. Two variables, one object. Programmers call a and b aliases for the same object.

steps.say: Now I drop five coins in through the tag marked b, and look through the tag marked a.

beats.say: The chest starts with 0 coins. I drop five in through the tag marked b, then look through the tag marked a.

wrong: Nothing — a has no coins, so it is an error
check.why: a and b refer to the same object, so a change made through either reference is seen through both.

steps.say: If I wanted a second, separate chest I would have to run new a second time. To count objects, count how many times new runs — not how many variables there are.

outro: “The next monster has tied two tags to one Counter. Find the single object and the rest is easy.”

question: Look closely at how b gets its value. What does the program print?
feedback: new runs once, so there is one Counter object. Counter b = a; copies the reference held in a, which makes b an alias: a second name for the same object. All three increment() calls therefore land on the same count, and both get() calls read it. For two independent counters, b would need its own new Counter().

feedback_template: new runs twice, so there are two objects. b = a makes b a second reference to the first object, which means the {{n}} calls through a and the {{m}} calls through b all raise the same count, giving {{expected}}. c refers to a separate object, so its {{k}} calls change nothing that a can see.

Objects are created by new, not by declaring variables. new Golem() runs once before the loop and once on each of the {{n}} passes through it, which makes {{expected}} objects. second = first and h = g only copy references, so they add names for objects that already exist.

question: The == operator is used on object variables here. What does the program print?
correct: false true
feedback: On object variables, == compares the references: it asks whether both sides refer to the very same object, and never looks inside. a and b came from two separate new expressions, so they are two objects and a == b is false even though both hold 4. c was copied from a, so both refer to one object and a == c is true.

correct: It prints false: a class that writes no equals gets a basic one that works like ==
incorrect: It prints true: equals compares two objects field by field, and both hold 4
It does not compile, because Gem declares no method named equals
It prints false because cut is private; a public cut would give true
feedback: Every class is handed a basic equals for free, so the call compiles. That free version knows nothing about your fields: it simply checks whether the two references lead to the same object, exactly as == does. a and b are separate objects, so the answer is false. To make equals compare contents, the class has to supply its own version. String does that, which is why equals works on text, and a record does it for you. Whether the field is private or public makes no difference.

correct: It throws a NullPointerException, because title still holds null
incorrect: It prints 0, because an unset String field is an empty string
It does not compile, because the constructor leaves title unassigned
It prints 4, because the word null is four characters long
feedback: The constructor sets name and never touches title, so title keeps the default for a field that refers to an object: null, meaning no object at all. The compiler does not insist that a constructor assign every field, so the class builds. getTitle() returns null without complaint; the crash comes one step later, when .length() is called on a reference that leads nowhere. Giving title a starting value, such as "" or "Novice", in the constructor prevents it.

question: A field or method marked {{1}} can be used only by code inside its own class. One marked {{2}} can be used by code in any class. One with no access modifier at all can be used by any class in the same {{3}}.
feedback: private is the tightest level and the normal choice for fields; public is the loosest and the normal choice for the methods other classes are meant to call. Leaving the modifier off gives package access: visible to the classes in the same package and to nobody else. A fourth level, protected, only makes sense once you have met inheritance.

question: Inside a class, declare a private int field named balance. Do not give it a starting value.
correct: private int balance;
feedback: The order is access modifier, then type, then name: private int balance;. Java rejects int private balance; and private balance int;. With no starting value the field begins at 0, the default for an int field.

correct: It does not compile: gold has private access in Vault
incorrect: It compiles, but throws an exception when the assignment runs
It compiles, but the assignment to gold is silently ignored
It compiles and stores 9999: private blocks code in other packages
feedback: private is enforced by the compiler, not while the program runs. Code outside Vault may not even mention v.gold, so the program is never built and there is nothing to throw an exception or to be ignored. Being in the same package does not help, because private means this class and no other. That is the point of encapsulation: the only way in is through the methods Vault chooses to offer.

question: A class Vault declares the field  private int gold;  Which statements about gold are true?
correct: Code in another class may not assign to it directly, even through a Vault variable
A method of Vault can read the gold of a different Vault object passed in as a parameter
incorrect: Its value is fixed once the constructor has finished running
It is shared between Vault objects, in the way a static field is
The class will not compile unless a constructor gives it a value
feedback: private controls WHO may touch a field, and nothing else. The boundary is the class, not the object, so a Vault method such as  boolean richerThan(Vault other)  may read other.gold. private does not freeze the value (that is final), does not share it between objects (that is static), and does not oblige a constructor to set it: an unassigned int field simply starts at 0.

question: The class Hero has the field  private int level;  Which method is a correctly written getter for it?
correct: public int getLevel() { return level; }
incorrect: public void getLevel() { System.out.println(level); }
public int getLevel(int level) { return level; }
public void getLevel() { return level; }
feedback: A getter RETURNS the field, so its return type is the field's type and it needs no parameters. Printing is not returning: the void version shows the number on the screen, but the caller cannot store it or compare it. The version with a parameter hands back whatever the caller passed in, because the parameter shadows the field. A void method that tries to return a value does not compile.

question: A {{1}} hands back the value of a private field and usually takes no parameters. A {{2}} takes one parameter, may check it before storing it, and usually has the return type {{3}}.
feedback: A getter (or accessor) reads: its return type matches the field and it needs no input. A setter (or mutator) writes: it receives the new value as a parameter, and since it has nothing to report back its return type is normally void. Because every change has to pass through the setter, the class gets the chance to refuse values that make no sense.

question: NPC: A setter that says no
intro: Zoya's kiln glows in the corner of the workshop. “An apprentice once set this to five thousand degrees,” they say. “Once. Then I rewrote the class.”

steps.say: heat is private, so no outside code can write k.heat = 5000. The only way in is the setter, and the setter looks at the new value before storing it. Checking a value before accepting it is called validation.

beats.say: Here is my Kiln class. The field heat is private, so no outside code can write k.heat = 5000.
The only way in is the setter, setHeat, and it looks at the new value before storing it. Checking a value before you accept it is called validation.

steps.say: Two calls: one sensible, one not.

beats.say: A new Kiln k starts at 200. Then two calls arrive: one sensible, one not.

check.why: 650 passes the if, so it is stored. 5000 fails it, the assignment is skipped, and the field keeps the last good value.

steps.say: A rejected value leaves the field exactly as it was. That is what encapsulation buys you: a private field plus a validating setter means the object can never hold a nonsense value, whoever calls it.

outro: “The next monster's setter guards a hero's hit points. Take the calls one at a time and ask each: does this value get in?”

question: This setter validates the new value before storing it. What does the program print?
feedback: Take the calls one at a time. 120 is above 100, so the if is false and hp stays 10. 45 is inside the range, so hp becomes 45. -5 is below 0, so it is refused and hp stays 45. The last call is not automatically the winner: only values that pass validation are stored.

feedback_template: balance starts at 100. deposit({{a}}) passes its check, giving {{mid}}. deposit(-{{b}}) fails amount > 0 and is ignored. withdraw({{w}}) is positive and no more than the balance, so it goes through and leaves {{expected}}. withdraw(500) asks for more than the account holds, so it is refused and the balance stays at {{expected}}.

question: Which statements about getters and setters are true?
correct: A setter can refuse a bad value and leave the field as it was
A getter may compute what it returns, such as a full name built from two fields
A class may give a field a getter and deliberately leave out the setter
incorrect: A private field with a getter can be assigned from outside, as in h.getHp() = 5;
A setter has to be named set plus the field name, or the class will not compile
feedback: Getters and setters are ordinary methods, so they can contain any logic. A setter can validate; a getter can simply return the field (most do) or build its answer, as in return first + " " + last;. A field with a getter and no setter is read-only from outside, which is often exactly what you want. A getter hands back a copy of the value, not the field itself, so h.getHp() = 5; does not compile. The names getHp and setHp are a convention people and tools rely on; the compiler does not care.

question: NPC: One tally for the whole workshop
intro: A slate hangs by the workshop door with a single chalk number on it. “Every golem carries its own power,” Zoya says. “But that slate? There is one of it, and it belongs to the workshop, not to any golem.”

steps.say: power is an instance field: every Golem object gets its own copy. made is marked static, so it belongs to the class itself. There is exactly one made, however many golems exist — it is the slate by the door.

beats.say: Two fields, and one word makes them very different.

power is an instance field: every Golem object gets its own copy. made is marked static, so it belongs to the class itself. There is exactly ONE made, however many golems exist. It is the slate by the door.

steps.say: Every run of the constructor adds 1 to that single shared field.

beats.say: Each run of the constructor adds 1 to that single shared field. I shape three golems:

check.why: All three constructors raised the same static field, so it reads 3. The powers 4, 9 and 2 live in three separate instance fields and never touch it.

steps.say: Look at the call: Golem.getMade() — class name, dot, method. A static method needs no object. The price is that it has no this, so it cannot read an instance field such as power: which golem's power would it mean?

outro: “The next monster numbers its tickets with a static field. Keep two columns as you trace: one for the class, one for each object.”

question: One of these fields is static and the other is not. What does the program print?
feedback: issued is static: one shared field for the whole class, raised by every constructor call, so it ends at 3. number is an instance field: each ticket copies the value issued had at the moment that ticket was made, and keeps it. a was first and holds 1; c was third and holds 3. Later tickets do not change a's number, because that copy belongs to a alone.

feedback_template: count is an instance field, so a's own count only sees a's {{n}} calls. total is static, one field shared by the whole class, so it sees every call made on any Counter: {{n}} and {{m}} together make {{total}}. Both are ints, so + adds them, and the line prints {{expected}}.

correct: report() is static, so it runs with no particular Hero, and there is no hp to read
incorrect: hp is private, so even a method of Hero needs a getter in order to read it
report() is void, and a void method is not allowed to print a field's value
hp gets its value where it is declared, when a constructor should assign it
feedback: A static method belongs to the class and can be called as Hero.report() before a single Hero exists. hp is an instance field, so there is one per object, and inside report() Java has no object to take it from. The compiler says: non-static variable hp cannot be referenced from a static context. Remove static from report(), or pass a Hero in as a parameter. private is not the problem, since methods of Hero may use Hero's private fields; void methods print things all the time; and giving a field its value where it is declared is perfectly legal.

question: The class Dice has a static method named roll that takes no arguments. From a different class, write the statement that calls it without creating a Dice object. Ignore the value it returns.
correct: Dice.roll();
Dice.roll()
feedback: A static method is called through the class: class name, dot, method name. No object is needed, so there is no new. You have been doing this all along with Math.sqrt(...) and Integer.parseInt(...). new Dice().roll() would build an object only to throw it away.

question: You are writing a Hero class for a game. Match each kind of variable to the piece of data it suits.

pairs.definition: One hero's current hit points, remembered between method calls
How many heroes the program has created so far
A running total needed only while one method adds up a hero's loot
The amount of damage a caller hands to takeDamage(...)

feedback: Ask who owns the data and how long it has to live. Data each object must remember is an instance field. Data about the class as a whole, of which there is exactly one, is a static field. A value needed only during one method call is a local variable, gone when the method returns (and with no default value). A value the caller supplies for that call is a parameter.

correct: Dog@1b6d3586
incorrect: Rex
rex
Dog[name=Rex]
feedback: println asks the object for its toString(). A class that writes none gets a basic one: the class name, an @, and a hexadecimal number that says nothing about the fields (the number varies from run to run). Java does not guess that name is the interesting field, and the object has no idea what its variable is called. Dog[name=Rex] is what you would get if Dog were a record. For an ordinary class you write toString yourself.

question: This class supplies its own toString. What does the program print?
correct: Elixir x3
feedback: println(p) calls p.toString() for you, and this class has replaced the basic Potion@... version with one that builds a readable string: name, then " x", then doses. The same call happens whenever an object is joined to a String with +. The @Override line asks the compiler to check that the method really does replace an existing one, so a slip such as tostring() is caught instead of silently ignored.

correct: A constructor that takes x and y
Accessor methods named x() and y()
A toString() giving text like Point[x=3, y=7]
An equals() that compares x and y
incorrect: Getter methods named getX() and getY()
Setter methods named setX() and setY()
feedback: A record is a compact way to declare a class whose whole job is to hold some values. From the header Java generates private final fields, a constructor taking every component, accessors named after the components with no get prefix, so p.x() and not p.getX(), plus toString, equals and hashCode based on the values. It writes no setters, because a record's fields are final: a record object does not change after it is built.

question: A record can have methods of its own as well as the ones Java writes for it. What does the program print?
feedback: new Point(3, 7) uses the constructor Java generated from the record header. p.x() is the generated accessor for the component x, giving 3. sum() is an ordinary method written inside the record's braces; it reads the two fields and returns their total. A record is a full class, with the repetitive parts written for you.

question: Both points are created separately with the same values. What does the program print?
correct: true false
feedback: A record gets an equals() that compares the components, and 2, 3 matches 2, 3, so a.equals(b) is true. == is never redefined by anything: it still asks whether a and b are the same object, and two new expressions made two objects, so it is false. Use equals() to ask whether two objects hold the same data.

correct: p = new Point(5, p.y());
incorrect: p.setX(5);
feedback: A record's fields are private and final, so an existing Point can never be altered: p.x = 5; does not compile, no setX was generated, and the accessor x() takes no arguments. To "change" a record you build a new one from the old values and point the variable at it. Objects that cannot change are called immutable, and they are safe to share: an alias cannot alter one behind your back.

question: An enum is a type with a fixed list of named values. What does the program print?
correct: SILVER 1 3
feedback: Printing an enum constant shows its name, so r gives SILVER. ordinal() is the constant's position in the declaration, counted from 0 as with array indexes: BRONZE 0, SILVER 1, GOLD 2. Rank.values() returns an array of all the constants, and there are 3 of them.

correct: A misspelt value such as Rank.SLIVER is rejected by the compiler
incorrect: New ranks can be added to Rank while the program is running
Two Rank values have to be compared with equals(), which is safer than ==
A Rank field is not able to hold null, which a String field can
feedback: A String field accepts any text, so "SLIVER" or "gold " slips through and the bug appears much later. A Rank field can hold one of the three constants and nothing else, and a name that is not on the list is a compile error. The list is fixed when the program is compiled; it cannot grow while the program runs. Each constant exists exactly once, so == is the normal, safe way to compare enum values. A Rank field can still be null, and like any field that refers to an object it starts that way.

question: An enum can have methods, and a switch can cover its constants one by one. What does the program print?
feedback: Inside bonus(), this is whichever constant the method was called on. The switch expression gives 20 for GOLD, 1 for BRONZE and 20 for GOLD again, so total ends at 41. The switch needs no default because it names every constant of the enum; add a fourth rank later and the compiler will point at this switch until you deal with it.

question: Coin supplies its own equals, which compares values. The loop counts two different things. What does the program print?
feedback: new runs four times, so there are four Coin objects, and target is a different object from every coin in the purse: c == target is never true and same stays 0. equals() has been written to compare value, and two of the purse's coins hold 5, so equal reaches 2. Notice that equals reads c.value, the private field of another Coin: private means private to the class, not to one object. (A class that writes its own equals should also write a matching hashCode; records do both for you.)

question: Both static methods receive the same Hero. What does the program print?
feedback: Calling a method copies the reference in a into the parameter h, so inside the method h is an alias for the caller's object. heal() uses that alias to change the object itself, and the caller sees hp rise from 50 to 60. swap() only points its own copy, h, at a brand-new Hero; the caller's variable a was never touched and still refers to the first object. The 99-hp hero is dropped when swap() returns.
